hook_text: Chicken gets expensive... and BEEF sales explode. Markets gossip. Here's how.
clip_script: Bird flu hits and chicken jumps to ninety-five. In the beef market, something odd happens: beef's own price hasn't moved, yet more people want beef this week than last week. Picture beef's demand curve — price up the side, quantity along the bottom, the curve sloping down. It does not slide along itself; the whole curve steps to the right, because at every beef price there are now more willing buyers. Rival's price up, my demand up — that is the substitute signature. Partners work the other way: if braai packs get pricey, charcoal sales sink even though charcoal's price never moved. Rivals move together. Partners move apart.
visual_style: Two shelf tags side by side — chicken's price spinning upward while a queue of shoppers slides over to the beef fridge; a demand curve stepping right like a dance move.
pacing: Quick setup, freeze on the odd fact, then the rule lands twice like a chorus.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for complements, factor markets and the four market structures.
